noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: describe how nervous and hormonal communication control responses and understand the differences between the two systems

primer.text: You already know that nerves carry fast electrical signals and that glands release chemicals into the blood. This note puts the two control systems side by side — nervous and hormonal — so you can name the messenger, the route, the speed and the duration of each, and pick the right system for any response an exam question describes.

lessons.title: The nervous system: electrical impulses at speed
lessons.opening: Two control systems share the job of responding to change: the nervous system and the hormonal (endocrine) system. The nervous side sends electrical impulses along neurones at speeds reaching about 100 metres per second, which is why a hand jerks back from a flame before you have thought about it. Speed is its defining feature.
keyPoints: Humans run two control systems side by side: nervous and hormonal (endocrine).
Electrical impulses race along neurones at speeds reaching 100 metres per second.
That speed makes nervous control ideal for instant responses such as the withdrawal reflex.
Receptors, the central nervous system's decision-making centres, and effectors are all coordinated by this system.

low.restatement: The nervous system uses fast electrical impulses along neurones, so responses happen almost instantly.
low.analogy: It is the body's lightning network — instant messages, instant reactions.
low.examPointer: Quote the speed figure (up to 100 m/s) when asked why nervous responses are rapid.

medium.restatement: Electrical signalling lets receptors, CNS decision centres and effectors act as one coordinated loop for functions needing immediacy.
medium.analogy: Compare it with a landline phone call — direct, wired and immediate, unlike a letter in the post.
medium.examPointer: Link speed to the reflex example: the flame-withdrawal case shows why some functions cannot wait for hormones.

check.stem: At roughly what top speed do impulses travel along neurones?

options.text: Up to about 100 metres per second
options.explanation: That is the stated top speed of nerve impulses.

options.text: Up to about 10 metres per second
options.explanation: An order of magnitude too slow.

options.text: Up to about 100 metres per hour
options.explanation: Wrong time unit — impulses are far faster.

options.text: Up to about 1000 metres per second
options.explanation: Overshoots the stated figure tenfold.

check.stem: What form does the message take inside the nervous system?

options.explanation: That is the endocrine route, not the nervous one.
Nervous messages are electrical impulses on nerve cells.
No such transmission exists in this system.
That is transport of gas, not of information.

check.stem: Which example shows the rapid response the nervous system makes possible?

options.explanation: Growth is slow and developmental, not a nervous response.

options.text: Jerking a hand back the instant it touches a flame
options.explanation: The withdrawal reflex is the named rapid-response example.
Digestion is chemical and slow.

options.text: Healing a cut over a week
options.explanation: Repair takes days and is not nervous control.

check.stem: Which set of components does the nervous system coordinate?

options.text: Sensory receptors, central decision-making centres and effectors
options.explanation: All three are coordinated in one loop by the nervous system.
Glands belong to the hormonal side of the comparison.

options.text: Only the muscles of the legs
options.explanation: The loop is body-wide, not limited to limbs.
Blood cells are carriers, not coordinated responders here.

check.stem: Which function is best handled by nervous rather than hormonal control?

options.text: Adjusting body chemistry over many hours
options.explanation: Slow adjustments suit hormones.
Growth is developmental, not instant control.

options.text: An instant withdrawal from a hot surface
options.explanation: Instant responses are exactly the nervous system's specialty.
Metabolic pacing suits hormonal control.

check.stem: State the message type and the cells that carry it in the nervous system.
check.modelAnswer: Electrical impulses, carried along nerve cells called neurones.

check.stem: Give the top speed at which impulses travel.
check.modelAnswer: Up to about 100 metres per second.

check.stem: Explain why a withdrawal reflex cannot rely on hormonal communication.
check.modelAnswer: Hormones move at blood-flow speed and must circulate before acting, whereas an impulse reaches about 100 metres per second along neurones; a hand on a flame would be burned before any hormone could arrive, so only electrical signalling is fast enough for protection.

check.stem: A student's finger brushes a hot kettle and pulls away at once. Name the route the fastest signal took and the organs that acted as effector.
check.modelAnswer: The signal ran as electrical impulses along sensory neurones into the central nervous system and out along motor neurones; the effectors were the arm muscles, which contracted to withdraw the finger.

lessons.title: The endocrine system and the head-to-head comparison
sourceHeadings: A comparison of the nervous and endocrine systems table
lessons.opening: The endocrine system works by chemistry. Endocrine glands secrete hormones into the blood, which carries them everywhere, and each hormone acts on its specific target organs to change their activity. Because transport relies on circulation, hormonal control is slower than nerves, but its effects last longer and spread wider.
keyPoints: The endocrine system sends information as chemical messengers called hormones.
Hormones travel in the blood plasma and so reach the whole body.
Each hormone acts on one or more named target organs and changes what they do.
Endocrine glands produce and secrete the hormones.
Hormonal control suits functions that do not need instant responses.

low.restatement: Glands release hormones into the bloodstream; each chemical signal acts on target organs, working more slowly but lasting longer than nerve impulses.
low.analogy: Hormones are letters delivered by the postal service — slower than a phone call, but read by every addressed office.
low.examPointer: For comparison questions anchor on the table: electrical vs chemical, neurones vs bloodstream, fast vs slower, local vs widespread, brief vs lasting.

medium.restatement: Because hormones circulate, one secretion can touch many organs at once and persist until breakdown, trading speed for breadth and duration.
medium.analogy: A radio broadcast reaches every receiver in range and keeps repeating, while a phone call reaches exactly one listener.
medium.examPointer: Duration wording matters: hormonal effects last until the hormone is broken down — quote that clause.

check.stem: How do hormones travel around the body?

options.explanation: Neurones carry electrical impulses, not hormones.
Hormones are carried by the blood and circulate body-wide.
The named route is the bloodstream.
No such tubes exist; glands release into blood.

check.stem: What kind of message does the endocrine system send?

options.explanation: That is the nervous system's medium.
Hormones are the chemical substances of endocrine control.
No acoustic signalling exists between organs.
Light is a stimulus, not an internal message.

check.stem: On what does a hormone act once it circulates?

options.explanation: Effects are specific to target organs, not universal.
Hormones alter the activity of specific target organs.

options.text: On the gland that released it only
options.explanation: The action happens at targets elsewhere in the body.
Hormones act on target organs of many kinds.

check.stem: Which pairing from the nervous-versus-endocrine comparison is correct?

options.text: Nervous message is chemical; endocrine message is electrical
options.explanation: The types are the wrong way round.

options.text: Nervous effect is widespread; endocrine effect is localised
options.explanation: Reversed — hormones act widely, nerves locally.

options.text: Nervous action is very fast; endocrine action is slower
options.explanation: That is the speed-of-action row of the table.

options.text: Nervous effects last long; endocrine effects stop quickly
options.explanation: Reversed duration — hormones last longer.

check.stem: Why do hormonal effects outlast nervous ones?

options.text: Because hormones continue acting until they are broken down
options.explanation: Duration ends only when the hormone is broken down.

options.text: Because nerves fire for hours at a time
options.explanation: Nervous effects stop quickly.

options.text: Because hormones replicate inside target cells
options.explanation: Hormones do not reproduce.
Glands secrete chemicals, not impulses.

check.stem: State what endocrine glands produce and the collective name for them.
check.modelAnswer: They produce and secrete hormones; together the glands form the endocrine system.

check.stem: Give the two message-transmission routes named in the comparison table.
check.modelAnswer: Nervous messages travel along neurones; hormonal messages travel through the bloodstream in plasma.

check.stem: Explain why one hormone secretion can affect several organs at once.
check.modelAnswer: Because hormones ride the circulating blood, a single secretion is delivered to every organ the blood reaches; any organ with matching target receptors responds, so one signal can change the activity of several targets simultaneously — unlike a nerve impulse, which is aimed along specific neurones.

check.stem: During a long walk your heart rate stays elevated for many minutes. Which control system fits this sustained adjustment, and why?
check.modelAnswer: The hormonal (endocrine) system fits: sustained adjustments suit chemical messengers that circulate and keep acting until broken down, whereas nervous control is reserved for instant, short-lived commands.

glossary.definition: A nerve cell that transmits electrical impulses; nerves are bundles of neurones.
The rapid automatic pull-away of a body part from danger, such as a hand leaving a flame.
A chemical messenger carried by the blood that changes the activity of specific target organs.
A group of cells that produces and secretes hormones into the bloodstream.
